en: Generosity, kind speech, courage and a sense of what is proper are four inborn qualities; they cannot be gained by practice.
One who leaves his own people and goes to live with others comes to ruin by himself, as a kingdom is ruined by injustice.

An elephant is huge, yet a small goad controls it; a lamp drives away darkness, yet it is small; a thunderbolt brings down mountains, yet it is small. The one whose inner power shines is the strong one; why trust in mere size?
In the age of Kali, after ten thousand years Lord Hari leaves the earth; after half that time the water of the Ganga leaves it; and after half of that the village gods leave.

first: गृहासक्तस्य नो विद्या न दया मांस भोजिनः ।
en: One attached to his home gains no learning, a meat-eater has no compassion, one greedy for money has no truth, and a man chasing women has no purity.
A wicked person does not become good however much he is taught; a neem tree does not turn sweet even if its roots are watered with milk and ghee.
A wicked person with filth inside is not made clean even by a hundred baths at holy places, just as a pot that held liquor is not made clean even by burning.

first: न वेत्ति तो यस्य गुण प्रकर्ष
en: It is no wonder that one who cannot see another's excellence always looks down on him; a forest woman throws away a pearl from an elephant's head and wears red berries instead.

first: ये तु संवत्सरं पूर्ण नित्यं मौनेन भुंजते ।
en: Those who eat their meals in silence every day for a whole year are honoured in heaven for countless ages.
A student should avoid these eight: lust, anger, greed, love of tasty food, love of adornment, too much fun, too much sleep, and too much flattery of others.
A Brahmin who lives on wild fruits and roots that no one has farmed, who always loves the forest, and who makes offerings to the ancestors every day is called a sage.
A Brahmin who is content with one meal a day, always busy with his six duties, and goes to his wife only at the proper time is called twice-born.
A Brahmin who is busy with worldly work, looks after cattle, and does trade and farming is called a Vaishya.
A Brahmin who sells lac, oil, indigo, safflower, honey, ghee, liquor and meat is called a Shudra.
A Brahmin who spoils others' work, is a hypocrite, serves only himself, cheats, hates others, and is soft outside but cruel inside is called a cat.
A Brahmin who without a thought destroys step-wells, wells, ponds, gardens and temples is called a barbarian.
A Brahmin who steals what belongs to the gods or to his teacher, who lays hands on another man's wife, and who lives off all creatures is called an outcast.

Good people should give away food and wealth and never hoard them; the fame of Karna, Bali and King Vikrama lives on even today. See how the bees, whose long-stored honey was lost without being given or enjoyed, rub their feet together in regret.
